title: To run on Jupiter’s weak sunlight, Europa Clipper needs solar wings 30 metres across

cover.alt: In a huge white clean room, a tall dark folded solar array stands beside the Europa Clipper spacecraft, with technicians in clean suits nearby.

body: At Jupiter, sunlight is only about **4% as strong** as it is near Earth, so a spacecraft that runs on solar power there needs enormous panels. NASA’s Europa Clipper, the largest interplanetary spacecraft the agency has launched, carries two arrays that give it a span of 30.5 m (100 ft), yet at Jupiter they will make only about 600 watts. Engineers chose solar power because it was cheaper than a plutonium generator and still practical. After a 2.9-billion-kilometre voyage it is due at Jupiter in April 2030, to fly past the icy moon Europa again and again, at times just 25 km above its surface.

slides.alt: A wide view of a white clean room: a tall stack of dark solar panels beside the spacecraft swings open panel by panel into a long flat wing of solar cells, while technicians in blue suits stand by on the floor.

slides.heading: At Jupiter, sunlight is only about 4% as strong as it is in Earth’s orbit
slides.note: Jupiter is about five times farther from the Sun than Earth is

slides.prompt: Europa Clipper’s solar wings span 30.5 metres. How much power will they make at Jupiter?
slides.detail: Near Earth the same panels would make far more. Out at Jupiter they have to catch every bit of the faint sunlight.

events.text: Due: a gravity boost from Earth

slides.question: Why did engineers give Europa Clipper solar panels instead of a nuclear power source?
options: Solar was cheaper and still practical
Nuclear power is banned in space
The panels shield it from radiation
slides.explanation: Solar power was cheaper than a plutonium-fuelled generator and practical to use, even with sunlight at Jupiter only about 4% as strong as near Earth.
